summary: Old Scituate Light on Cedar Point: a granite tower of 1811, dark from 1860 to 1994, bought back by the town, and relit in 2024 after a restored lantern room.

structures.note: Split-granite octagonal tower of about 25 ft (7.6 m) (LighthouseFriends; USLHS gives 49 ft to lantern center, not the same)
Brick superstructure about 15 ft (4.6 m) added in 1827 (NRHP; LighthouseFriends)
One-and-a-half-story keeper's house built with the tower; a private residence today (NSRWA)
Lantern room removed in October 2022 and replaced; lifted into place 15 November 2023 (LighthouseFriends)

access.note: Outdoor visitors are welcome year-round on the grounds and the walkway by the harbor. Occasional tours are run by the Scituate Historical Society. The keeper's house is a private residence (NSRWA).

facts.agency: Scituate Historical Society (manages and gives tours; USLHS and NSRWA list it as owner); the Town of Scituate owned the property from 1917 (NRHP, LighthouseFriends)

events.note: Congress appropriates $4,000 for a lighthouse at Scituate (LighthouseFriends; the NRHP chronology records 2 3/4 acres purchased in 1810)
Granite tower and wooden keeper's house built for $3,200 by three men from Hingham; finished in September 1811 (LighthouseFriends)
Some sources say first lit September 1811; a Notice to Mariners of January 1812 gives 1 April 1812 (LighthouseFriends). USLHS year established: 1811
British landing party at Scituate during the War of 1812; the keeper's daughters Rebecca and Abigail Bates play the fife and drum and the British withdraw, according to family and local tradition
Brick extension about 15 ft added to the granite tower; new lantern room; a second, red light shown from windows lower in the tower (NRHP; LighthouseFriends)
Refit with plate glass and fourteen-inch reflectors; the tower keeps its white and red lights (LighthouseFriends)
Engineer I.W.P. Lewis inspects the light and says it is confused with Boston Light, a cause of wrecks on Cohasset rocks (as quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Minot's Ledge Light (the first) destroyed in a storm on 16 April 1851 (LighthouseFriends) or 17 April (NRHP); the Scituate light regains temporary service
Fourth-order Fresnel lens (LighthouseFriends)
Light discontinued after the new Minot's Ledge light entered service on 15 November 1860 (NRHP gives 14 November as the last lighting of the old light)
Lantern room and Fresnel lens removed; property leased (LighthouseFriends)
Separate light on the end of the breakwater first shown on 10 June 1891 (Lighthouse Board report, LighthouseFriends)
Act of 28 June 1916 authorises sale of the former lighthouse reservation to the Town of Scituate as a historic landmark
Town acquires the property: $1,000 plus $1,500 for land to the southeast (NRHP); LighthouseFriends says the town raised $4,000
New lantern room (replica) built atop the tower, at the start of the Depression (LighthouseFriends)
Scituate Historical Society appropriates $6,500 for repairs (NSRWA)
Tower vacated and vandalized (NRHP chronology)
Town meeting gives the Scituate Historical Society management of the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends; NSRWA)
Relighted as a private aid to navigation after 134 years of darkness (LighthouseFriends)
Outer course of poor-quality bricks found badly deteriorated and replaced (LighthouseFriends)
Stone revetment completed to protect the lighthouse from storms (LighthouseFriends)
Town meeting backs a $2 million restoration in April 2022; old lantern room removed October 2022 (LighthouseFriends)
New copper-clad lantern room lifted into place on 15 November 2023 (LighthouseFriends)
Relighting held 7 August 2024, National Lighthouse Day (LighthouseFriends)
Watershed association: light removed from service, put back two years later; NRHP chronology says it shared duties with the first Minot's Ledge light in 1850
Relit with a light visible from land only (NSRWA); visible from sea in 1994

corrections.proposed: tower, granite (octagonal), built 1811, about 7.6 m (25 ft); brick superstructure about 4.6 m (15 ft) built 1827
corrections.why: The 15.0 m in the record is the brick superstructure's height in feet (15 ft, about 4.6 m), not metres. The 1811 tower was split granite; the brick extension was added in 1827.

corrections.proposed: Owner unclear: the Town of Scituate held the property from 1917 (NRHP 1981 owner line; LighthouseFriends); the Scituate Historical Society manages it since 1968 and is listed as owner/manager by USLHS and NSRWA

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The 1811 granite tower, the 1827 brick extension and the 1994 private relight are three stages of the same structure. The record's conflict is over the first light date, which LighthouseFriends reports as September 1811 in some sources and 1 April 1812 in a Notice to Mariners.

notes_for_editor: 1) Ownership: NRHP 1981 owner line (Town of Scituate); LighthouseFriends (town acquired 1917; Society management from 1968); USLHS and NSRWA (Scituate Historical Society as owner/manager). Not settled; the story says the Society manages and gives tours and that the town held the property from 1917. 2) Purchase: NRHP chronology says 2 3/4 acres purchased in 1810; LighthouseFriends says the plot was seized under eminent domain from an owner who later blocked access. 3) First light: September 1811 (some sources, LighthouseFriends) against 1 April 1812 (Notice to Mariners, as LighthouseFriends prints it). Wikipedia lead gives 19 September 1811 (not cited). 4) Tower height: record says 15.0 m for the brick part; NRHP says 15 ft. 5) The 1900-1924 roster lines (Prouty, Stubeck, Cushman) are listed by the archive under this station, but the tower was discontinued in 1860 and the 1891 breakwater light is a separate aid; no source read ties these men to the old tower. They may be keepers of the breakwater light; the archive's own listing is kept, unresolved. 6) Thomas Richardson: roster ends 1859; NRHP and LighthouseFriends say he was keeper when the light went out in November 1860. 7) Rebecca and Abigail Bates (1814) are not on the archive roster; their 'in charge' stint comes from LighthouseFriends, which says research indicates the story is likely true and that the ship was confused. The NRHP chronology and NSRWA both repeat the story as local tradition. 8) The Lewis 1842 and Osborne quotations are as LighthouseFriends prints them from Lighthouse Board and Auditor reports that were not read directly. 9) No Chronicling America search was run; the War of 1812 episode rests on the three secondary accounts. 10) Living people: the two later caretakers (a live-in caretaker who retired in 2008 after 22 years, and the family chosen in 2008, whose blog is public) are not named in the story; the story gives only their caretaking role. 11) Characteristic and focal height: the Wikipedia lead (flashing white 15s; focal height 15 m) is not cited, so neither is in facts. The record's values were not checked against the Light List. 12) Today: the Scituate Historical Society's own site returned HTTP 403; its 2026 open-house listing was seen only in search results and is not cited. 13) Lantern room: LighthouseFriends says a new copper-clad lantern room was lifted on 15 November 2023; the replica lantern of 1930 is in the events. Fact-check 2026-10-22, disagreements now stated in the story: (a) the 1814 hiding place: 1981 form says behind a hill, LighthouseFriends and NSRWA say cedars; (b) La Hogue: LighthouseFriends says the sisters saw her, and also says records place her elsewhere; (c) the 1850-1852 gap in service (NSRWA) against the NRHP's 1850 shared duties; (d) 1917 price: $4,000 (LighthouseFriends, NSRWA) against $1,000 plus $1,500 (NRHP); (e) relight: 1991 land-visible, 1994 sea-visible (NSRWA) against 1994 (LighthouseFriends); (f) ownership: Town of Scituate (NRHP 1981, LighthouseFriends) against the society (NSRWA, USLHS). The story no longer calls ownership unsettled without giving both. The caretaker family's blog plan is left out (a private family, not a fact about the station). The 2008 caretakers are not named. The NSRWA says the keeper's house is a private residence; LighthouseFriends says the dwelling is closed to visitors and that the keepers' family lives in it. The breakwater light, the 1900-1924 roster names and the 1950s NSRWA shipwreck (Etrusco, 16 March 1956, NSRWA) are not used; the Etrusco wreck is a possible addition if a source ties it to the station more closely.
